steps.body:
The population has one fixed number — the **parameter**, p. You never see it.

What you see is a **statistic**, p̂: the answer your particular sample happened to give. Draw a new sample and you get a new p̂.

The truth stands still. The estimate moves. Every idea in this course is about how much it moves.
60% of this town really does support the plan. You do not know that — you only get to poll.

widget.prompt: Keep the poll at 25 people and run at least 20 of them. Watch where the answers land.
widget.successFeedback: Every one of those polls was honest, random and correctly conducted — and they still disagree with each other by 20 points or more. That scatter is sampling variability, and it is not a mistake anyone made.
widget.wrongSizeFeedback: Come back to the 25-person poll for now. The point of this step is to see how far apart honest polls of the SAME size can land.
widget.moreDrawsFeedback: A few polls cannot show you the scatter. Run more — the pattern only appears once there is a crowd of them.

predict.prompt: You'll run 20 honest, random polls of 25 people each, from a population where 60% say yes. The results will land…

options.label: All within a point or two of 60%

predict.reveal: Honest same-size polls disagree — here by 20 points or more — with nobody making a mistake. That scatter is sampling variability, and it's why one poll is never the whole story.

cml.actionGoal: Run repeated random samples and coordinate sample size with center and sampling variability.

explanationVariants: Every poll used the same honest method. They differ because each one happened to catch a different 25 people — that is sampling variability, not error.
The parameter (60%) never moved during the simulation. Only the statistic moved.

widget.prompt: Your 20 polls of 25 people gave answers spread over roughly 40 points. What does that tell you?

options.label: Honest random samples disagree with each other — the estimate wobbles even when nothing is wrong.
options.feedback: Right. This scatter is built into sampling, and the whole subject is about measuring it rather than pretending it away.

options.label: Some of those polls were conducted badly.
options.feedback: None of them was. They used the same random method — they simply caught different people, and different people answer differently.

options.label: The true support level keeps changing.
options.feedback: The truth sat at 60% the whole time, marked by the dashed line. The town did not change its mind between your polls.

options.label: The polls are biased, since so many missed 60%.
options.feedback: Bias would push the pile to one side of the truth. Look at it: the dots land on both sides, centred on 60%. That is variability, not bias.

explanationVariants: The parameter describes the whole population and is fixed. The statistic describes your one sample and changes every time you sample again.
You compute a statistic; you can only estimate a parameter.

widget.prompt: Match each quantity to what it is.

left.label: p̂ = 0.68, from your neighbour's poll of 25

right.label: the parameter — fixed, unknown, one of it
a statistic — known, and it moved
another statistic — same method, different answer

pairErrors.feedback: The town's true support is not something you computed from a sample — it is the fixed thing you are trying to estimate.
Your poll's 0.56 came from 25 people, so it is a statistic. Poll again and it changes; a parameter never does.

widget.missFeedback: Ask: did this number come from the whole population (parameter) or from one sample (statistic)?
widget.successFeedback: One parameter, many statistics — and the statistics scatter around the parameter.

steps.body:
So a single poll is not "the answer". It is **one draw** from a whole spread of answers your method could have produced.

That spread is the thing worth studying. It has a shape, a centre, and a width — and each of those tells you something you can act on.

explanationVariants: An honest random method overshoots as often as it undershoots, so the pile centres on the true value. That property is called being unbiased.
Centred on the truth is exactly what bias-free means — it does not mean any single poll is right.

widget.prompt: Your 20 honest polls landed on both sides of 60%. What does the CENTRE of that pile tell you?

options.label: The method is unbiased — it misses in both directions equally, so it centres on the truth.
options.feedback: Right. Unbiased is a property of the method, not of any single poll.

options.label: Each individual poll is accurate.
options.feedback: Most of them missed by several points. Unbiasedness is about the pile as a whole, not about any one dot in it.

options.label: The polls were too small.
options.feedback: The centre would sit on 60% for any size. Size changes the WIDTH of the pile, not where it sits — which is the next lesson.

options.label: Nothing — a centre is just an average.
options.feedback: It is the most important average in the subject: it says the method is aimed at the truth. A biased method centres somewhere else.

hints: Both pollsters used honest random samples of the same size. Ask what could make two honest polls differ.
Sampling variability alone routinely produces gaps of this size at n = 25 — you just watched it happen.
So neither pollster needs to have made a mistake, and neither one is 'the real number'.
explanationVariants: Two honest polls of 25 people can easily differ by 12 points through sampling variability alone, so the disagreement is not evidence that anyone erred.
Each poll is one dot from the same pile. Dots in a pile disagree with each other; that is what a pile is.

widget.prompt: Two pollsters use identical honest methods and 25-person random samples. One reports 52%, the other 64%. Who made a mistake?

options.label: Neither — a 12-point gap between honest 25-person polls is ordinary sampling variability.
options.feedback: Right. You saw that scatter with your own hands. The fix is not to accuse anyone; it is to report the wobble alongside the number.

options.label: The one who reported 52% — the true value is higher.
options.feedback: In the real world you do not know the true value, so you cannot convict a poll by comparing it with a truth you cannot see.

options.label: Both — honest polls should agree.
options.feedback: Honest polls agree only about the method, never about the exact number. Disagreement of this size is expected at n = 25, not evidence of malpractice.

options.label: Whichever one had the smaller sample.
options.feedback: Their samples are the same size. And in any case a smaller sample is not a wrong sample — it is a wobblier one.

takeaways: The parameter p is fixed and unseen; the statistic p̂ is computed and moves with every sample.
Honest random samples disagree with each other. That scatter is sampling variability, not error.
An unbiased method produces a pile centred on the truth — even though almost none of its individual polls hit it.
steps.teaser: Next: change the sample size and watch the pile change shape.

concept.body: Ask where the number came from. From every member of the population? Then it is a parameter — fixed, and usually unknowable. From the people you happened to ask? Then it is a statistic — knowable, and different every time you ask again.

explanationVariants: "43% of the 200 students we surveyed" is computed from a sample, so it is a statistic.
Survey another 200 students and the 43% will move. Parameters do not move.

widget.prompt: "43% of the 200 students we surveyed walk to school." Parameter or statistic?

options.label: A statistic — it came from a sample.
options.feedback: Right, and it would come out differently with a different 200 students.

options.label: A parameter — it is a percentage of students.
options.feedback: Being a percentage is not the test. The test is whether it came from the whole population or from a sample. This one came from 200 people.
